question: At the Olympic games that introduced women's boxing, there were 6 countries with the biggest discrepancy between gold and bronze medals won. I'd like to know which of the countries went on to achieve a higher medal count at the 2016 Rio games, and which of those countries had competed in the fewest Olympics as of 2022.

Based on my research, here's what I found:

## Women's Boxing Introduction
Women's boxing made its Olympic debut at the **2012 London Games**.

## Countries with Biggest Gold-Bronze Discrepancies in Women's Boxing (2012)

At the 2012 London Olympics, in the women's boxing event (which had 3 weight classes), the medal breakdown by country was:

| Country | Gold | Bronze | Discrepancy (G-B) |
|---------|------|--------|-------------------|
| Great Britain | 3 | 1 | **+2** |
| Russia | 1 | 3 | **-2** |
| Brazil | 0 | 2 | **-2** |
| Azerbaijan | 0 | 2 | **-2** |
| Ireland | 1 | 2 | **-1** |
| Kazakhstan | 1 | 2 | **-1** |
| India | 0 | 1 | **-1** |
| China | 1 | 1 | **0** |
| USA | 1 | 1 | **0** |
| Tajikistan | 0 | 1 | **-1** |

The six countries with the largest discrepancies were **Great Britain (+2), Russia (-2), Brazil (-2), Azerbaijan (-2), Ireland (-1), and Kazakhstan (-1)**.

## Which Achieved Higher Medal Count in 2016 Rio?

Comparing their **total Olympic medal counts** (all sports) from 2012 vs. 2016:

| Country | 2012 Medals | 2016 Medals | Improvement |
|---------|-------------|-------------|-------------|
| Great Britain | 65 | 67 | ✅ +2 |
| Russia | 13 | 24 | ✅ +11 |
| Brazil | 9 | 22 | ✅ +13 |
| Azerbaijan | 7 | 5 | ❌ -2 |
| Ireland | 13 | 17 | ✅ +4 |
| Kazakhstan | 11 | 17 | ✅ +6 |

**Five countries achieved higher medal counts in 2016**: Great Britain, Russia, Brazil, Ireland, and Kazakhstan. Azerbaijan actually declined.

## Which Competed in Fewest Olympics as of 2022?

Among the five qualifying countries:
- **Great Britain**: First appeared 1896, competed in EVERY Olympics (~30+ total)
- **Russia**: First appeared 1900 (as Romanov Empire/Soviet Union), continued through present (~28+ total)
- **Brazil**: First appeared 1920 (~24+ total)
- **Ireland**: First appeared 1896 (~28+ total)
- **Kazakhstan**: First appeared 1994 (after independence) (~9-10 total Summer + Winter)

**Answer: Kazakhstan** has competed in the fewest Olympic Games among these countries.

🏆 **Summary**: Among the six countries with the biggest gold-bronze discrepancy in women's boxing at 2012, **five achieved higher medal counts in Rio 2016** (excluding Azerbaijan). Of those five, **Kazakhstan** has competed in the fewest Olympics overall as of 2022.

Although women have participated in boxing for almost as long as the sport has existed, female fights have been sometimes outlawed in boxing's history and athletic commissioners have sometimes refused to sanction or issue licenses to female boxers.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-3) Reports of women entering the ring go back to the 18th century.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Brown-4)

## Historical overview
[edit]
Bennett sisters boxing, c.1910–1915
Louise Adler, female lightweight world boxing champion of the 1920s, training for her title defense
One of the earliest mentions of women's boxing is in the travelogue of a German man who visited London in 1710. While taking in a men's boxing match, he met a woman in the audience who claimed to have previously boxed another woman in the same venue.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto16-5)
One of the earliest known women's boxing matches to have been advertised in print was in London between Elizabeth Wilkinson and Hannah Hyfield in 1722. Billing herself as the "European Championess", Wilkinson and her husband would also fight other mixed couples as a pair, with Wilkinson fighting the other woman, and her husband fighting the other man. In those days, the rules of boxing allowed kicking, gouging and other methods of attack not part of today's arsenal.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto9-6)
Women's boxing first appeared in the Olympic Games as a demonstration sport in 1904, in St. Louis.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto15-7)

## Historical overview
During the 1920s, Professor Andrew Newton formed a Women's Boxing Club in London.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto10-8) However women's boxing was hugely controversial. In early 1926, Shoreditch borough council banned an arranged exhibition match between boxers Annie Newton and Madge Baker, a student of Digger Stanley.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto7-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto1-11) An attempt to hold the match in nearby Hackney instead was defeated by a campaign led by the Mayor of Hackney, who wrote, "I regard this proposed exhibition of women boxers as a gratification of the sensual ideals of a crowd of vulgar men."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto1-11) The Home Secretary Sir William Joynson-Hicks was among those opposing the match, claiming "the Legislature never imagined that such a disgraceful exhibition would have been staged in this country."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto-9) The story was reported across the country[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto6-12) and even internationally.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto8-13)
In 1988 the Swedish Amateur Boxing Association sanctioned events for women.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto14-14)
In 1997 the British Amateur Boxing Association sanctioned its first boxing competition for women. The first event was meant to be between two thirteen-year-olds, but one of the boxers dropped out because of hostile media attention. A month later, an event was held between two sixteen-year-olds.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-15)

## Historical overview
The British Boxing Board of Control refused to issue licenses to women until they issued one to Jane Couch in 1998.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-BBC_1998-16) By the end of the century, however, they had issued five such licenses. The first sanctioned professional bout between women in the U.K. was in November 1998 at Streatham in London, between Jane Couch and Simona Lukic. Couch won.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto2-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto4-18)
Renata Cristina Dos Santos Ferreira punches Adriana Salles, São Paulo, Brazil (2006)
The International Boxing Association (amateur) accepted new rules for women's boxing at the end of the 20th century and approved the first European Cup for Women in 1999 and the first World Championship for women in 2001.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-19) In October 2001 the first women's world amateur boxing championships,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto12-20) called the [2001 Women's World Amateur Boxing Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Women's_World_Amateur_Boxing_Championships "2001 Women's World Amateur Boxing Championships"), were held in Scranton, in the United States.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto13-21)
Lucia Rijker and Jane Couch boxing, 2003

## Historical overview
Women's boxing was not featured at the 2008 Olympics; however, on 14 August 2009, it was announced that the International Olympic Committee's Executive Board (EB) had approved the inclusion of women's boxing for the Games in London in the 2012 Olympics,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-24) contrary to the expectations of some observers. Around these (2009) hearings, in conjunction with AIBA (International Boxing Association), the International Olympic Committee agreed to include three additional women's weight classes to the 2012 London Olympic Games. A new "gender-appropriate" women's boxing uniform was being created at the time, which would have required women (under AIBA rules) to wear skirts during competition. The issue was widely ignored by the public until amateur boxer and London student Elizabeth Plank brought the issue to light. She created a petition at Change.com to end the gender-based mandatory uniforms.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Paradis_82%E2%80%93109-25) It was eventually decided (before the 2012 Olympics) to give women boxers the option of wearing shorts or a skirt.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-26)

## Historical overview
Women were allowed to competitively box for the first time at the Olympics during the 2012 Summer Olympics, in London, producing the world's first 12 female Olympic medalist boxers.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto26-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto23-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto22-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto21-30)Nicola Adams of Great Britain won the world's first Olympic women's boxing gold medal.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-2012gold-31)
On 14 September 2014, after defeating Croatian Ivana Habazin, Cecilia Brækhus became the first Norwegian and the first woman to hold all major world championship belts in her weight division (welterweight) in boxing history.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto24-32)
In 2015 the World Boxing Federation unified various women's titles to have one title holder.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-33)

## Historical overview
In 2024, Cindy Ngamba became the first boxer chosen for the Refugee Olympic Team;[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-34) later that year she became the first medalist for the Refugee Olympic Team at the Olympics, having won bronze in [women's 75 kg boxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_75_kg "Boxing at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Women's 75 kg") at the 2024 Summer Olympics.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Cindyauto-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Ngambaauto1-37)
_See also: 2024 Summer Olympics boxing controversy_
On 9 August 2024, Algerian boxer Imane Khelif defeated Yang Liu of China in the final to win an Olympic gold medal.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Beacham_2024d-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Pierce_2024-39) Khelif therefore became Algeria's first female gold medalist in boxing, as well as the country's first boxer of any gender to win a medal since Mohamed Allalou in 2000[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Ouest-France_2024-40) and the first to win a gold medal since Hocine Soltani in 1996.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Beacham_2024d-38)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Dotson_2024-41)

## Historical overview
Khelif had been disqualified from the [2023 Women's World Boxing Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_IBA_Women's_World_Boxing_Championships "2023 IBA Women's World Boxing Championships") organized by the Russian-led International Boxing Association (IBA) after failing unspecified gender eligibility tests, along with boxer Lin Yu-ting.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto35-42) The International Olympic Committee (IOC) and its Paris Boxing Unit criticized the disqualification as "sudden and arbitrary" and taken "without any due process".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto36-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto34-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-BBC_News-2024-45)_The Washington Post_ stated, "It remains unclear what standards Khelif and Lin Yu Ting failed [in 2023] to lead to the disqualifications."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Carpenter-2024-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto33-47) The IBA did not reveal the testing methodology, stating the "specifics remain confidential".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Euronews-2024-48) The IBA's Olympic status was revoked in June 2023,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto32-49) due to governance issues and perceived judging and refereeing corruption.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Euronews-2024-48)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Ingle-2024-50)

## Historical overview
In 2019 English boxer Barbara Buttrick became one of the first three women boxers (and the first English woman boxer) elected to the International Boxing Hall of Fame; 2019 was the first year that women were on the ballot.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto19-118)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto20-119)
In 2021, Lauren Price became the first Welsh boxer of any gender to win an Olympic gold medal.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-159)[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-160)

## Historical overview
In 2022 two female boxers headlined at a major venue in the United Kingdom for the first time, which occurred at the O2 Arena. That fight was a title unification bout between Claressa Shields and Savannah Marshall. Shields won via unanimous decision with two judges scoring the fight 97–93 and one scoring it 96–94, all in favor of Shields to become the undisputed middleweight world champion.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-161)[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-162)[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-163)[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-164) As well, the fight headlined the first all-female boxing card in the United Kingdom.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-165) Later in the year, Chantelle Cameron defeated Jessica McCaskill in a match held in Abu Dhabi, making Cameron the undisputed world light-welterweight champion and the United Kingdom's first undisputed female boxing world champion.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-166)[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-167)
Natasha Jonas won the British Boxing Board of Control’s 2022 British Boxer of the Year award, which made her the first woman to win the British Boxing Board of Control's British Boxer of the Year Award.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-168)

## Historical overview
On 6 May 2023, Lauren Price won the first British women's title fight in professional boxing history, becoming the first female British welterweight champion and the first woman to receive a Lonsdale Belt, by defeating Kirstie Bavington by unanimous points victory.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-169)[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-170)[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-171)
In October 2023, Natasha Jonas became the first black woman to receive a manager's license from the British Boxing Board of Control.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-172)[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-173)
On 14 March 2024 it was announced that Lauren Price would challenge Jessica McCaskill for her WBA, IBO, and _Ring_ female welterweight World titles on 11 May 2024 in Cardiff, Wales.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-174)[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto28-175) Price won the contest by unanimous technical decision after an accidental clash of heads that took place in the fifth round caused an injury to McCaskill's eye and she was ruled unable to continue at the start of round nine. This win made Price Wales’ first female professional boxing world champion.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-176)[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto28-175)

## Historical overview
In 1876, the first women's boxing match was held in the United States. In this match Nell Saunders defeated Rose Harland. Her prize was $200 and a silver butter dish.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-177)[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-178)
Women's boxing first appeared in the Olympic Games as a demonstration sport in 1904, in St. Louis.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto15-7)
In 1954, Barbara Buttrick was part of the first boxing match between two women on American national television.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-179)[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto5-180)
In 1975, Caroline Svendsen became the first woman to receive a boxing license in the United States when she was granted one in Nevada.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto5-180)

## Historical overview
Also in 1975, Jackie Tonawanda sued the New York State Athletic Commission (NYSAC) for denying her a boxing license because of her gender.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-181) This resulted in the case _Garrett v. New York State Athletic Commission_ (1975) at the New York Supreme Court (Tonawanda was also known as Jacqueline Garrett) which was decided in her favor.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-womanauto-182) However, this did not overturn the law in New York against women boxing.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-183) But Cathy Davis sued the New York State Athletic Commission in 1977 because she was denied a boxing license because she was a woman, and the case was decided in her favor later that year, with the judge invalidating New York State rule number 205.15, which stated, "No woman may be licensed as a boxer or second or licensed to compete in any wrestling exhibition with men."[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-womanauto1-184)[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-185) In his opinion the judge cited the precedent set by _Garrett v. New York State Athletic Commission_ (1975), which "found the regulation invalid under the equal protection clauses of the State and Federal Constitutions".

## Historical overview
Dallas Malloy was denied an application by USA Boxing due to being female. She sued and U.S. District Judge Barbara Rothstein allowed her to box by granting a preliminary injunction.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto11-202) In October 1993, Malloy defeated Heather Poyner in the United States' first sanctioned amateur boxing match between two female boxers.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-203)[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-204)USA Boxing lifted its ban on women's boxing later in 1993.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto11-202)[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-205) When USA Boxing officially recognized women's boxing in 1993, it became the first organization to do so in the world.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-206)[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-latimes1993-207)
Also in 1993, Don King, the world-famous boxing promoter, signed American boxer Christy Martin in October,[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-208)[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-209) making Martin the first female boxer to sign with King.[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Christy:4-210)[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Martin:0-211)

## Historical overview
In 1995, the New York Golden Gloves allowed women boxers to compete for the first time.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto5-180)[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-212)
On March 16, 1996, a boxing match took place that is often called the fight that "put women's boxing on the map",[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-:Match13-213)[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2014194%E2%80%93209-214) or "the bout that made women's boxing".[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-:Match5-215) It was held in Nevada between American Christy Martin and Irishwoman Deirdre Gogarty. The fight was won by Martin, in a six rounds unanimous decision, and led to her featuring as the first female boxer on the cover of _Sports Illustrated_ on April 15, 1996;[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-:Martin12-216) the headline read, "The Lady Is a Champ".[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-217)
In October 2001 the first women's world amateur boxing championships,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto12-20) called the [2001 Women's World Amateur Boxing Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Women's_World_Amateur_Boxing_Championships "2001 Women's World Amateur Boxing Championships"), were held in Scranton, in the United States.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto13-21)

## Historical overview
In 2002 Canadian-born American boxing promoter Aileen Eaton became the first woman inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame.[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Aileenauto-218)
On April 2, 2005 Becky Zerlentes was participating in the Colorado State Boxing Senior Female Championships at the Denver Coliseum in Denver. She was knocked out in the third round by her opponent, Heather Schmitz, fell unconscious, and died without regaining consciousness. This made Zerlentes the first woman known to have died of injuries sustained during a sanctioned boxing match in the United States. According to the Denver County coroner the cause of death was blunt force trauma to the head.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-219)[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-220)

## Historical overview
Women were allowed to competitively box for the first time at the Olympics during the 2012 Summer Olympics in London, producing the world's first 12 female Olympic medalist boxers.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto26-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto23-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto22-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto21-30) At those Olympics, Claressa Shields became the first American woman to win a boxing gold medal.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-221) As well, Marlen Esparza became the first American woman to qualify for the Olympics in women's boxing when she qualified for those Olympics.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Esparzaauto1-222) She went on to defeat Karlha Magliocco, making her the first American woman winner of an Olympic boxing match,[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-223) and to win a bronze medal, making her the first American woman winner of any Olympic boxing medal.[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-224)
In 2014 the [International Women's Boxing Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Women's_Boxing_Hall_of_Fame "International Women's Boxing Hall of Fame"), located in America, held its first induction.[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-225)[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-226)

Boxing
Anne-Sophie Da Costa and Tina Rupprecht boxing in 2017  
Also known as Pugilism  
FocusPunching, Striking  
Olympic sport Yes, as of the 2012 Olympics
Although women have participated in boxing for almost as long as the sport has existed, female fights have been sometimes outlawed in boxing's history and athletic commissioners have sometimes refused to sanction or issue licenses to female boxers.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-3) Reports of women entering the ring go back to the 18th century.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Brown-4)
texts.1:
## Historical overview
[edit]
Bennett sisters boxing, c.1910–1915
Louise Adler, female lightweight world boxing champion of the 1920s, training for her title defense
One of the earliest mentions of women's boxing is in the travelogue of a German man who visited London in 1710. While taking in a men's boxing match, he met a woman in the audience who claimed to have previously boxed another woman in the same venue.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto16-5)
One of the earliest known women's boxing matches to have been advertised in print was in London between Elizabeth Wilkinson and Hannah Hyfield in 1722. Billing herself as the "European Championess", Wilkinson and her husband would also fight other mixed couples as a pair, with Wilkinson fighting the other woman, and her husband fighting the other man. In those days, the rules of boxing allowed kicking, gouging and other methods of attack not part of today's arsenal.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto9-6)
Women's boxing first appeared in the Olympic Games as a demonstration sport in 1904, in St. Louis.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto15-7)
texts.2:
## Historical overview
During the 1920s, Professor Andrew Newton formed a Women's Boxing Club in London.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto10-8) However women's boxing was hugely controversial. In early 1926, Shoreditch borough council banned an arranged exhibition match between boxers Annie Newton and Madge Baker, a student of Digger Stanley.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto7-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto1-11) An attempt to hold the match in nearby Hackney instead was defeated by a campaign led by the Mayor of Hackney, who wrote, "I regard this proposed exhibition of women boxers as a gratification of the sensual ideals of a crowd of vulgar men."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto1-11) The Home Secretary Sir William Joynson-Hicks was among those opposing the match, claiming "the Legislature never imagined that such a disgraceful exhibition would have been staged in this country."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto-9) The story was reported across the country[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto6-12) and even internationally.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto8-13)
In 1988 the Swedish Amateur Boxing Association sanctioned events for women.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto14-14)
In 1997 the British Amateur Boxing Association sanctioned its first boxing competition for women. The first event was meant to be between two thirteen-year-olds, but one of the boxers dropped out because of hostile media attention. A month later, an event was held between two sixteen-year-olds.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-15)
texts.3:
## Historical overview
The British Boxing Board of Control refused to issue licenses to women until they issued one to Jane Couch in 1998.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-BBC_1998-16) By the end of the century, however, they had issued five such licenses. The first sanctioned professional bout between women in the U.K. was in November 1998 at Streatham in London, between Jane Couch and Simona Lukic. Couch won.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto2-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto4-18)
Renata Cristina Dos Santos Ferreira punches Adriana Salles, São Paulo, Brazil (2006)
The International Boxing Association (amateur) accepted new rules for women's boxing at the end of the 20th century and approved the first European Cup for Women in 1999 and the first World Championship for women in 2001.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-19) In October 2001 the first women's world amateur boxing championships,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto12-20) called the [2001 Women's World Amateur Boxing Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Women's_World_Amateur_Boxing_Championships "2001 Women's World Amateur Boxing Championships"), were held in Scranton, in the United States.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto13-21)
Lucia Rijker and Jane Couch boxing, 2003
texts.4:
## Historical overview
Women's boxing was not featured at the 2008 Olympics; however, on 14 August 2009, it was announced that the International Olympic Committee's Executive Board (EB) had approved the inclusion of women's boxing for the Games in London in the 2012 Olympics,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-24) contrary to the expectations of some observers. Around these (2009) hearings, in conjunction with AIBA (International Boxing Association), the International Olympic Committee agreed to include three additional women's weight classes to the 2012 London Olympic Games. A new "gender-appropriate" women's boxing uniform was being created at the time, which would have required women (under AIBA rules) to wear skirts during competition. The issue was widely ignored by the public until amateur boxer and London student Elizabeth Plank brought the issue to light. She created a petition at Change.com to end the gender-based mandatory uniforms.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Paradis_82%E2%80%93109-25) It was eventually decided (before the 2012 Olympics) to give women boxers the option of wearing shorts or a skirt.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-26)
texts.5:
## Historical overview
Women were allowed to competitively box for the first time at the Olympics during the 2012 Summer Olympics, in London, producing the world's first 12 female Olympic medalist boxers.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto26-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto23-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto22-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto21-30)Nicola Adams of Great Britain won the world's first Olympic women's boxing gold medal.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-2012gold-31)
On 14 September 2014, after defeating Croatian Ivana Habazin, Cecilia Brækhus became the first Norwegian and the first woman to hold all major world championship belts in her weight division (welterweight) in boxing history.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto24-32)
In 2015 the World Boxing Federation unified various women's titles to have one title holder.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-33)
texts.6:
## Historical overview
In 2024, Cindy Ngamba became the first boxer chosen for the Refugee Olympic Team;[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-34) later that year she became the first medalist for the Refugee Olympic Team at the Olympics, having won bronze in [women's 75 kg boxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_75_kg "Boxing at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Women's 75 kg") at the 2024 Summer Olympics.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Cindyauto-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Ngambaauto1-37)
_See also: 2024 Summer Olympics boxing controversy_
On 9 August 2024, Algerian boxer Imane Khelif defeated Yang Liu of China in the final to win an Olympic gold medal.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Beacham_2024d-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Pierce_2024-39) Khelif therefore became Algeria's first female gold medalist in boxing, as well as the country's first boxer of any gender to win a medal since Mohamed Allalou in 2000[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Ouest-France_2024-40) and the first to win a gold medal since Hocine Soltani in 1996.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Beacham_2024d-38)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Dotson_2024-41)
texts.7:
## Historical overview
Khelif had been disqualified from the [2023 Women's World Boxing Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_IBA_Women's_World_Boxing_Championships "2023 IBA Women's World Boxing Championships") organized by the Russian-led International Boxing Association (IBA) after failing unspecified gender eligibility tests, along with boxer Lin Yu-ting.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto35-42) The International Olympic Committee (IOC) and its Paris Boxing Unit criticized the disqualification as "sudden and arbitrary" and taken "without any due process".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto36-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto34-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-BBC_News-2024-45)_The Washington Post_ stated, "It remains unclear what standards Khelif and Lin Yu Ting failed [in 2023] to lead to the disqualifications."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Carpenter-2024-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto33-47) The IBA did not reveal the testing methodology, stating the "specifics remain confidential".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Euronews-2024-48) The IBA's Olympic status was revoked in June 2023,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto32-49) due to governance issues and perceived judging and refereeing corruption.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Euronews-2024-48)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Ingle-2024-50)
texts.29:
## Historical overview
In 2019 English boxer Barbara Buttrick became one of the first three women boxers (and the first English woman boxer) elected to the International Boxing Hall of Fame; 2019 was the first year that women were on the ballot.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto19-118)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto20-119)
In 2021, Lauren Price became the first Welsh boxer of any gender to win an Olympic gold medal.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-159)[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-160)
texts.30:
## Historical overview
In 2022 two female boxers headlined at a major venue in the United Kingdom for the first time, which occurred at the O2 Arena. That fight was a title unification bout between Claressa Shields and Savannah Marshall. Shields won via unanimous decision with two judges scoring the fight 97–93 and one scoring it 96–94, all in favor of Shields to become the undisputed middleweight world champion.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-161)[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-162)[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-163)[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-164) As well, the fight headlined the first all-female boxing card in the United Kingdom.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-165) Later in the year, Chantelle Cameron defeated Jessica McCaskill in a match held in Abu Dhabi, making Cameron the undisputed world light-welterweight champion and the United Kingdom's first undisputed female boxing world champion.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-166)[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-167)
Natasha Jonas won the British Boxing Board of Control’s 2022 British Boxer of the Year award, which made her the first woman to win the British Boxing Board of Control's British Boxer of the Year Award.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-168)
texts.31:
## Historical overview
On 6 May 2023, Lauren Price won the first British women's title fight in professional boxing history, becoming the first female British welterweight champion and the first woman to receive a Lonsdale Belt, by defeating Kirstie Bavington by unanimous points victory.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-169)[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-170)[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-171)
In October 2023, Natasha Jonas became the first black woman to receive a manager's license from the British Boxing Board of Control.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-172)[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-173)
On 14 March 2024 it was announced that Lauren Price would challenge Jessica McCaskill for her WBA, IBO, and _Ring_ female welterweight World titles on 11 May 2024 in Cardiff, Wales.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-174)[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto28-175) Price won the contest by unanimous technical decision after an accidental clash of heads that took place in the fifth round caused an injury to McCaskill's eye and she was ruled unable to continue at the start of round nine. This win made Price Wales’ first female professional boxing world champion.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-176)[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto28-175)
texts.32:
## Historical overview
In 1876, the first women's boxing match was held in the United States. In this match Nell Saunders defeated Rose Harland. Her prize was $200 and a silver butter dish.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-177)[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-178)
Women's boxing first appeared in the Olympic Games as a demonstration sport in 1904, in St. Louis.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto15-7)
In 1954, Barbara Buttrick was part of the first boxing match between two women on American national television.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-179)[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto5-180)
In 1975, Caroline Svendsen became the first woman to receive a boxing license in the United States when she was granted one in Nevada.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto5-180)
texts.33:
## Historical overview
Also in 1975, Jackie Tonawanda sued the New York State Athletic Commission (NYSAC) for denying her a boxing license because of her gender.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-181) This resulted in the case _Garrett v. New York State Athletic Commission_ (1975) at the New York Supreme Court (Tonawanda was also known as Jacqueline Garrett) which was decided in her favor.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-womanauto-182) However, this did not overturn the law in New York against women boxing.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-183) But Cathy Davis sued the New York State Athletic Commission in 1977 because she was denied a boxing license because she was a woman, and the case was decided in her favor later that year, with the judge invalidating New York State rule number 205.15, which stated, "No woman may be licensed as a boxer or second or licensed to compete in any wrestling exhibition with men."[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-womanauto1-184)[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-185) In his opinion the judge cited the precedent set by _Garrett v. New York State Athletic Commission_ (1975), which "found the regulation invalid under the equal protection clauses of the State and Federal Constitutions".
texts.36:
## Historical overview
Dallas Malloy was denied an application by USA Boxing due to being female. She sued and U.S. District Judge Barbara Rothstein allowed her to box by granting a preliminary injunction.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto11-202) In October 1993, Malloy defeated Heather Poyner in the United States' first sanctioned amateur boxing match between two female boxers.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-203)[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-204)USA Boxing lifted its ban on women's boxing later in 1993.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto11-202)[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-205) When USA Boxing officially recognized women's boxing in 1993, it became the first organization to do so in the world.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-206)[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-latimes1993-207)
Also in 1993, Don King, the world-famous boxing promoter, signed American boxer Christy Martin in October,[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-208)[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-209) making Martin the first female boxer to sign with King.[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Christy:4-210)[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Martin:0-211)
texts.37:
## Historical overview
In 1995, the New York Golden Gloves allowed women boxers to compete for the first time.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto5-180)[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-212)
On March 16, 1996, a boxing match took place that is often called the fight that "put women's boxing on the map",[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-:Match13-213)[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2014194%E2%80%93209-214) or "the bout that made women's boxing".[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-:Match5-215) It was held in Nevada between American Christy Martin and Irishwoman Deirdre Gogarty. The fight was won by Martin, in a six rounds unanimous decision, and led to her featuring as the first female boxer on the cover of _Sports Illustrated_ on April 15, 1996;[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-:Martin12-216) the headline read, "The Lady Is a Champ".[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-217)
In October 2001 the first women's world amateur boxing championships,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto12-20) called the [2001 Women's World Amateur Boxing Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Women's_World_Amateur_Boxing_Championships "2001 Women's World Amateur Boxing Championships"), were held in Scranton, in the United States.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto13-21)
texts.38:
## Historical overview
In 2002 Canadian-born American boxing promoter Aileen Eaton became the first woman inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame.[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Aileenauto-218)
On April 2, 2005 Becky Zerlentes was participating in the Colorado State Boxing Senior Female Championships at the Denver Coliseum in Denver. She was knocked out in the third round by her opponent, Heather Schmitz, fell unconscious, and died without regaining consciousness. This made Zerlentes the first woman known to have died of injuries sustained during a sanctioned boxing match in the United States. According to the Denver County coroner the cause of death was blunt force trauma to the head.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-219)[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-220)

Women were allowed to competitively box for the first time at the Olympics during the 2012 Summer Olympics in London, producing the world's first 12 female Olympic medalist boxers.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto26-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto23-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto22-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto21-30) At those Olympics, Claressa Shields became the first American woman to win a boxing gold medal.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-221) As well, Marlen Esparza became the first American woman to qualify for the Olympics in women's boxing when she qualified for those Olympics.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Esparzaauto1-222) She went on to defeat Karlha Magliocco, making her the first American woman winner of an Olympic boxing match,[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-223) and to win a bronze medal, making her the first American woman winner of any Olympic boxing medal.[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-224)

Although women have participated in boxing for almost as long as the sport has existed, female fights have been sometimes outlawed in boxing's history and athletic commissioners have sometimes refused to sanction or issue licenses to female boxers.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-3) Reports of women entering the ring go back to the 18th century.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Brown-4)

## Historical overview
[edit]
Bennett sisters boxing, c.1910–1915
Louise Adler, female lightweight world boxing champion of the 1920s, training for her title defense
One of the earliest mentions of women's boxing is in the travelogue of a German man who visited London in 1710. While taking in a men's boxing match, he met a woman in the audience who claimed to have previously boxed another woman in the same venue.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto16-5)
One of the earliest known women's boxing matches to have been advertised in print was in London between Elizabeth Wilkinson and Hannah Hyfield in 1722. Billing herself as the "European Championess", Wilkinson and her husband would also fight other mixed couples as a pair, with Wilkinson fighting the other woman, and her husband fighting the other man. In those days, the rules of boxing allowed kicking, gouging and other methods of attack not part of today's arsenal.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto9-6)
Women's boxing first appeared in the Olympic Games as a demonstration sport in 1904, in St. Louis.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto15-7)

## Historical overview
During the 1920s, Professor Andrew Newton formed a Women's Boxing Club in London.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto10-8) However women's boxing was hugely controversial. In early 1926, Shoreditch borough council banned an arranged exhibition match between boxers Annie Newton and Madge Baker, a student of Digger Stanley.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto7-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto1-11) An attempt to hold the match in nearby Hackney instead was defeated by a campaign led by the Mayor of Hackney, who wrote, "I regard this proposed exhibition of women boxers as a gratification of the sensual ideals of a crowd of vulgar men."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto1-11) The Home Secretary Sir William Joynson-Hicks was among those opposing the match, claiming "the Legislature never imagined that such a disgraceful exhibition would have been staged in this country."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto-9) The story was reported across the country[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto6-12) and even internationally.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto8-13)
In 1988 the Swedish Amateur Boxing Association sanctioned events for women.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto14-14)
In 1997 the British Amateur Boxing Association sanctioned its first boxing competition for women. The first event was meant to be between two thirteen-year-olds, but one of the boxers dropped out because of hostile media attention. A month later, an event was held between two sixteen-year-olds.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-15)

## Historical overview
The British Boxing Board of Control refused to issue licenses to women until they issued one to Jane Couch in 1998.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-BBC_1998-16) By the end of the century, however, they had issued five such licenses. The first sanctioned professional bout between women in the U.K. was in November 1998 at Streatham in London, between Jane Couch and Simona Lukic. Couch won.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto2-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto4-18)
Renata Cristina Dos Santos Ferreira punches Adriana Salles, São Paulo, Brazil (2006)
The International Boxing Association (amateur) accepted new rules for women's boxing at the end of the 20th century and approved the first European Cup for Women in 1999 and the first World Championship for women in 2001.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-19) In October 2001 the first women's world amateur boxing championships,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto12-20) called the [2001 Women's World Amateur Boxing Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Women's_World_Amateur_Boxing_Championships "2001 Women's World Amateur Boxing Championships"), were held in Scranton, in the United States.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto13-21)
Lucia Rijker and Jane Couch boxing, 2003

## Historical overview
Women's boxing was not featured at the 2008 Olympics; however, on 14 August 2009, it was announced that the International Olympic Committee's Executive Board (EB) had approved the inclusion of women's boxing for the Games in London in the 2012 Olympics,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-24) contrary to the expectations of some observers. Around these (2009) hearings, in conjunction with AIBA (International Boxing Association), the International Olympic Committee agreed to include three additional women's weight classes to the 2012 London Olympic Games. A new "gender-appropriate" women's boxing uniform was being created at the time, which would have required women (under AIBA rules) to wear skirts during competition. The issue was widely ignored by the public until amateur boxer and London student Elizabeth Plank brought the issue to light. She created a petition at Change.com to end the gender-based mandatory uniforms.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Paradis_82%E2%80%93109-25) It was eventually decided (before the 2012 Olympics) to give women boxers the option of wearing shorts or a skirt.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-26)

## Historical overview
Women were allowed to competitively box for the first time at the Olympics during the 2012 Summer Olympics, in London, producing the world's first 12 female Olympic medalist boxers.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto26-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto23-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto22-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto21-30)Nicola Adams of Great Britain won the world's first Olympic women's boxing gold medal.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-2012gold-31)
On 14 September 2014, after defeating Croatian Ivana Habazin, Cecilia Brækhus became the first Norwegian and the first woman to hold all major world championship belts in her weight division (welterweight) in boxing history.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto24-32)
In 2015 the World Boxing Federation unified various women's titles to have one title holder.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-33)

## Historical overview
In 2024, Cindy Ngamba became the first boxer chosen for the Refugee Olympic Team;[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-34) later that year she became the first medalist for the Refugee Olympic Team at the Olympics, having won bronze in [women's 75 kg boxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_75_kg "Boxing at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Women's 75 kg") at the 2024 Summer Olympics.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Cindyauto-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Ngambaauto1-37)
_See also: 2024 Summer Olympics boxing controversy_
On 9 August 2024, Algerian boxer Imane Khelif defeated Yang Liu of China in the final to win an Olympic gold medal.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Beacham_2024d-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Pierce_2024-39) Khelif therefore became Algeria's first female gold medalist in boxing, as well as the country's first boxer of any gender to win a medal since Mohamed Allalou in 2000[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Ouest-France_2024-40) and the first to win a gold medal since Hocine Soltani in 1996.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Beacham_2024d-38)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Dotson_2024-41)

## Historical overview
Khelif had been disqualified from the [2023 Women's World Boxing Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_IBA_Women's_World_Boxing_Championships "2023 IBA Women's World Boxing Championships") organized by the Russian-led International Boxing Association (IBA) after failing unspecified gender eligibility tests, along with boxer Lin Yu-ting.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto35-42) The International Olympic Committee (IOC) and its Paris Boxing Unit criticized the disqualification as "sudden and arbitrary" and taken "without any due process".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto36-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto34-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-BBC_News-2024-45)_The Washington Post_ stated, "It remains unclear what standards Khelif and Lin Yu Ting failed [in 2023] to lead to the disqualifications."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Carpenter-2024-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto33-47) The IBA did not reveal the testing methodology, stating the "specifics remain confidential".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Euronews-2024-48) The IBA's Olympic status was revoked in June 2023,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto32-49) due to governance issues and perceived judging and refereeing corruption.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Euronews-2024-48)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Ingle-2024-50)

## Historical overview
In 2019 English boxer Barbara Buttrick became one of the first three women boxers (and the first English woman boxer) elected to the International Boxing Hall of Fame; 2019 was the first year that women were on the ballot.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto19-118)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto20-119)
In 2021, Lauren Price became the first Welsh boxer of any gender to win an Olympic gold medal.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-159)[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-160)

## Historical overview
In 2022 two female boxers headlined at a major venue in the United Kingdom for the first time, which occurred at the O2 Arena. That fight was a title unification bout between Claressa Shields and Savannah Marshall. Shields won via unanimous decision with two judges scoring the fight 97–93 and one scoring it 96–94, all in favor of Shields to become the undisputed middleweight world champion.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-161)[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-162)[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-163)[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-164) As well, the fight headlined the first all-female boxing card in the United Kingdom.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-165) Later in the year, Chantelle Cameron defeated Jessica McCaskill in a match held in Abu Dhabi, making Cameron the undisputed world light-welterweight champion and the United Kingdom's first undisputed female boxing world champion.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-166)[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-167)
Natasha Jonas won the British Boxing Board of Control’s 2022 British Boxer of the Year award, which made her the first woman to win the British Boxing Board of Control's British Boxer of the Year Award.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-168)

## Historical overview
On 6 May 2023, Lauren Price won the first British women's title fight in professional boxing history, becoming the first female British welterweight champion and the first woman to receive a Lonsdale Belt, by defeating Kirstie Bavington by unanimous points victory.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-169)[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-170)[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-171)
In October 2023, Natasha Jonas became the first black woman to receive a manager's license from the British Boxing Board of Control.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-172)[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-173)
On 14 March 2024 it was announced that Lauren Price would challenge Jessica McCaskill for her WBA, IBO, and _Ring_ female welterweight World titles on 11 May 2024 in Cardiff, Wales.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-174)[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto28-175) Price won the contest by unanimous technical decision after an accidental clash of heads that took place in the fifth round caused an injury to McCaskill's eye and she was ruled unable to continue at the start of round nine. This win made Price Wales’ first female professional boxing world champion.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-176)[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto28-175)

## Historical overview
In 1876, the first women's boxing match was held in the United States. In this match Nell Saunders defeated Rose Harland. Her prize was $200 and a silver butter dish.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-177)[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-178)
Women's boxing first appeared in the Olympic Games as a demonstration sport in 1904, in St. Louis.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto15-7)
In 1954, Barbara Buttrick was part of the first boxing match between two women on American national television.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-179)[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto5-180)
In 1975, Caroline Svendsen became the first woman to receive a boxing license in the United States when she was granted one in Nevada.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto5-180)

## Historical overview
Also in 1975, Jackie Tonawanda sued the New York State Athletic Commission (NYSAC) for denying her a boxing license because of her gender.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-181) This resulted in the case _Garrett v. New York State Athletic Commission_ (1975) at the New York Supreme Court (Tonawanda was also known as Jacqueline Garrett) which was decided in her favor.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-womanauto-182) However, this did not overturn the law in New York against women boxing.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-183) But Cathy Davis sued the New York State Athletic Commission in 1977 because she was denied a boxing license because she was a woman, and the case was decided in her favor later that year, with the judge invalidating New York State rule number 205.15, which stated, "No woman may be licensed as a boxer or second or licensed to compete in any wrestling exhibition with men."[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-womanauto1-184)[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-185) In his opinion the judge cited the precedent set by _Garrett v. New York State Athletic Commission_ (1975), which "found the regulation invalid under the equal protection clauses of the State and Federal Constitutions".

## Historical overview
Dallas Malloy was denied an application by USA Boxing due to being female. She sued and U.S. District Judge Barbara Rothstein allowed her to box by granting a preliminary injunction.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto11-202) In October 1993, Malloy defeated Heather Poyner in the United States' first sanctioned amateur boxing match between two female boxers.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-203)[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-204)USA Boxing lifted its ban on women's boxing later in 1993.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto11-202)[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-205) When USA Boxing officially recognized women's boxing in 1993, it became the first organization to do so in the world.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-206)[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-latimes1993-207)
Also in 1993, Don King, the world-famous boxing promoter, signed American boxer Christy Martin in October,[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-208)[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-209) making Martin the first female boxer to sign with King.[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Christy:4-210)[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Martin:0-211)

## Historical overview
In 1995, the New York Golden Gloves allowed women boxers to compete for the first time.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto5-180)[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-212)
On March 16, 1996, a boxing match took place that is often called the fight that "put women's boxing on the map",[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-:Match13-213)[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2014194%E2%80%93209-214) or "the bout that made women's boxing".[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-:Match5-215) It was held in Nevada between American Christy Martin and Irishwoman Deirdre Gogarty. The fight was won by Martin, in a six rounds unanimous decision, and led to her featuring as the first female boxer on the cover of _Sports Illustrated_ on April 15, 1996;[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-:Martin12-216) the headline read, "The Lady Is a Champ".[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-217)
In October 2001 the first women's world amateur boxing championships,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto12-20) called the [2001 Women's World Amateur Boxing Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Women's_World_Amateur_Boxing_Championships "2001 Women's World Amateur Boxing Championships"), were held in Scranton, in the United States.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto13-21)

## Historical overview
In 2002 Canadian-born American boxing promoter Aileen Eaton became the first woman inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame.[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Aileenauto-218)
On April 2, 2005 Becky Zerlentes was participating in the Colorado State Boxing Senior Female Championships at the Denver Coliseum in Denver. She was knocked out in the third round by her opponent, Heather Schmitz, fell unconscious, and died without regaining consciousness. This made Zerlentes the first woman known to have died of injuries sustained during a sanctioned boxing match in the United States. According to the Denver County coroner the cause of death was blunt force trauma to the head.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-219)[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-220)

## Historical overview
Women were allowed to competitively box for the first time at the Olympics during the 2012 Summer Olympics in London, producing the world's first 12 female Olympic medalist boxers.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto26-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto23-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto22-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-auto21-30) At those Olympics, Claressa Shields became the first American woman to win a boxing gold medal.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-221) As well, Marlen Esparza became the first American woman to qualify for the Olympics in women's boxing when she qualified for those Olympics.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-Esparzaauto1-222) She went on to defeat Karlha Magliocco, making her the first American woman winner of an Olympic boxing match,[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-223) and to win a bronze medal, making her the first American woman winner of any Olympic boxing medal.[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-224)
In 2014 the [International Women's Boxing Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Women's_Boxing_Hall_of_Fame "International Women's Boxing Hall of Fame"), located in America, held its first induction.[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-225)[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_boxing#cite_note-226)

# Boxing
## Description
Boxing was contested at the Ancient Olympic Games and many other sporting festivals in Ancient Greece. Boxing was then an even more brutal sport, as the combatants wore leather thongs on their hands. Originally, the thongs were simple straps of leather, but later they were reinforced with sharp pieces of metal, and the glove was called a _cestus_. The first known Ancient Olympic boxing champion was Onomastos of Smyrna, who won in 688 BCE and 684 BCE. The last known was Varasdates of Armenia, in 369 CE, who was one of the last known champions of the Ancient Olympic Games. Professional boxing has been around since the early 18th century, with a recognized list of professional champions dating from the late 1700s.
Men’s boxing made its first Olympic appearance at St. Louis 1904. All the entrants were Americans, and the event doubled as the AAU Championships for that year. Boxing was again contested at the 1908 Olympics in London. In 1912, boxing could not be on the Olympic Programme because the sport required special permits in Sweden at that time. Since Antwerpen 1920, boxing has been on the programme of every edition of the Olympic Games.
The United States was originally the premier nation in Olympic boxing. In the last 40 years, it has faced tough competition, first by the Soviet Union, and, more recently, by Cuba. However, as of 2024, the USA still leads the medal table with 118 medals and 50 golds, followed by Cuba, with 80 medals and 42 golds.
Three male boxers have won three Olympic gold medals: Hungary’s László Papp, and Teófilo Stevenson and Félix Savón of Cuba. A number of Olympic boxers have gone on to become professional World Champions, notably Cassius Clay (Muhammad Ali), George Foreman, Joe Frazier, Sugar Ray Leonard, Floyd Mayweather, Jr., Volodymyr Klychko, Oscar De La Hoya, and Lennox Lewis.

# Boxing
## Description
Women’s boxing made its Olympic début only at London 2012. Great Britain’s Nicola Adams, American Claressa Shields, and Ireland’s Kellie Harrington currently lead the women’s classification, all with two golds. China’s Li Qian is the only female boxer with three Olympic medals, one of each color.
Boxing is also part of the Youth Summer Olympics, with the first boys’ events contested at its inaugural edition of Singapore 2010, and the first girls’ boxing events staged in its second edition, at Nanjing 2014.
Until recently, amateur boxing was governed by the International Boxing Association (IBA), which was originally called the Association Internationale de Boxe Amateur (AIBA), founded on 29 and 30 November 1946. Although the name change happened in 2007, the association still used the acronym AIBA until December 2021, when it was rebranded to the IBA.
AIBA succeeded the Fédération Internationale de Boxe Amateur (FIBA), which had been founded on 24 August 1920 in Antwerpen, during the Olympics, with 11 founding members. Before having its own organization, boxing was governed together with tug-of-war, weight throwing, weightlifting, and wrestling in the Internationaler Weltverband für Schwerathletik (1912-1920).
After a years-long dispute fueled by defying advice and instructions from the International Olympic Committee (IOC), the International Boxing Association was banished from the Olympic Family on 22 June 2023. The dispute centered on the IBA’s management under presidents from Uzbekistan and Russia who the IOC disapproved of, its finances being backed by Russian state energy firm Gazprom, plus the integrity of bouts and judging. Nevertheless, the sport still appeared at Paris 2024, with the IOC serving as the sport’s governing body during the Olympics.

# Boxing
## Description
Despite its long Olympic history, boxing was still not on the programme for Los Angeles 2028 until the formal recognition of a new governing body, World Boxing, by the IOC on 20 March 2025. As of January 2026, World Boxing has 155 member National Federations (123 Full Members, one Associate Member, and 31 Endorsed Members). The Los Angeles Games will witness the same number of weight classes for men and women, creating gender parity in the sport for the first time ever.

# Boxing
## Description
Boxing was contested at the Ancient Olympic Games and many other sporting festivals in Ancient Greece. Boxing was then an even more brutal sport, as the combatants wore leather thongs on their hands. Originally, the thongs were simple straps of leather, but later they were reinforced with sharp pieces of metal, and the glove was called a _cestus_. The first known Ancient Olympic boxing champion was Onomastos of Smyrna, who won in 688 BCE and 684 BCE. The last known was Varasdates of Armenia, in 369 CE, who was one of the last known champions of the Ancient Olympic Games. Professional boxing has been around since the early 18th century, with a recognized list of professional champions dating from the late 1700s.
Men’s boxing made its first Olympic appearance at St. Louis 1904. All the entrants were Americans, and the event doubled as the AAU Championships for that year. Boxing was again contested at the 1908 Olympics in London. In 1912, boxing could not be on the Olympic Programme because the sport required special permits in Sweden at that time. Since Antwerpen 1920, boxing has been on the programme of every edition of the Olympic Games.
The United States was originally the premier nation in Olympic boxing. In the last 40 years, it has faced tough competition, first by the Soviet Union, and, more recently, by Cuba. However, as of 2024, the USA still leads the medal table with 118 medals and 50 golds, followed by Cuba, with 80 medals and 42 golds.
Three male boxers have won three Olympic gold medals: Hungary’s László Papp, and Teófilo Stevenson and Félix Savón of Cuba. A number of Olympic boxers have gone on to become professional World Champions, notably Cassius Clay (Muhammad Ali), George Foreman, Joe Frazier, Sugar Ray Leonard, Floyd Mayweather, Jr., Volodymyr Klychko, Oscar De La Hoya, and Lennox Lewis.

# Boxing
## Description
Women’s boxing made its Olympic début only at London 2012. Great Britain’s Nicola Adams, American Claressa Shields, and Ireland’s Kellie Harrington currently lead the women’s classification, all with two golds. China’s Li Qian is the only female boxer with three Olympic medals, one of each color.
Boxing is also part of the Youth Summer Olympics, with the first boys’ events contested at its inaugural edition of Singapore 2010, and the first girls’ boxing events staged in its second edition, at Nanjing 2014.
Until recently, amateur boxing was governed by the International Boxing Association (IBA), which was originally called the Association Internationale de Boxe Amateur (AIBA), founded on 29 and 30 November 1946. Although the name change happened in 2007, the association still used the acronym AIBA until December 2021, when it was rebranded to the IBA.
AIBA succeeded the Fédération Internationale de Boxe Amateur (FIBA), which had been founded on 24 August 1920 in Antwerpen, during the Olympics, with 11 founding members. Before having its own organization, boxing was governed together with tug-of-war, weight throwing, weightlifting, and wrestling in the Internationaler Weltverband für Schwerathletik (1912-1920).
After a years-long dispute fueled by defying advice and instructions from the International Olympic Committee (IOC), the International Boxing Association was banished from the Olympic Family on 22 June 2023. The dispute centered on the IBA’s management under presidents from Uzbekistan and Russia who the IOC disapproved of, its finances being backed by Russian state energy firm Gazprom, plus the integrity of bouts and judging. Nevertheless, the sport still appeared at Paris 2024, with the IOC serving as the sport’s governing body during the Olympics.

# Boxing
## Description
Despite its long Olympic history, boxing was still not on the programme for Los Angeles 2028 until the formal recognition of a new governing body, World Boxing, by the IOC on 20 March 2025. As of January 2026, World Boxing has 155 member National Federations (123 Full Members, one Associate Member, and 31 Endorsed Members). The Los Angeles Games will witness the same number of weight classes for men and women, creating gender parity in the sport for the first time ever.
